summary:
Karl Dietrich Bracher (1922–2016) was a German political scientist and historian best known for his studies of the Weimar Republic and Nazi Germany. After serving in the Wehrmacht and being captured in Tunisia in 1943, he earned a doctorate in classics at the University of Tübingen, studied at Harvard, and taught at the Free University of Berlin and the University of Bonn.

Bracher’s central concern was how democracies can be preserved. In *The Disintegration of the Weimar Republic* (1955), he argued that Germany’s democracy did not collapse inevitably or simply because of economic pressures, Versailles, or impersonal historical forces. Rather, political leaders made deliberate choices that weakened constitutional government, particularly by relying on presidential emergency powers instead of parliament. He described the process as a loss of democratic power, a resulting power vacuum, and finally the Nazi seizure of power. His interpretation challenged historians who viewed presidential rule as a necessary effort to save democracy.

Bracher emphasized human responsibility and the importance of human rights, pluralism, constitutional government, and democratic citizenship. Though he rejected the idea that German history followed an inevitable “special path” to Nazism, he argued that German political traditions and authoritarian ideas helped make the Nazi regime possible. In works including *The German Dictatorship* (1969), he treated Nazism as a totalitarian system built through human choices, and criticized Marxist explanations that reduced it to capitalist interests as well as accounts that minimized Hitler’s agency. His combination of historical research and political science was influential and often controversial. Bracher was also co-publisher of the *Quarterly Journal of Contemporary History* from 1978. He married Dorothee Schleicher in 1951; they had two children.
